body:
Biotechnology as a dual-use field

Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or biological components to develop useful products and processes. Traditional biotechnology includes activities such as fermentation, while modern biotechnology also includes applications based on molecular biology and genetic information.

Biotechnology is relevant to agriculture, public health, medicine, environmental protection and national defence. A medical diagnostic system used during a civilian disease outbreak may also be useful for protecting personnel working in difficult conditions.

Basic biological concepts

DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, carries hereditary information in most living organisms. A gene is a functional unit of hereditary information associated with a particular biological product or function.

Genetic engineering involves deliberate modification of genetic material using biotechnology methods. It is different from simply observing a natural biological characteristic.

Recombinant DNA technology involves joining genetic material from different sources for specified applications. At the school level, its importance lies in understanding that biological information can be studied and used to produce useful products, including certain medical substances.

How biotechnology supports health and preparedness

  • Diagnostics: Tests that help identify a disease or biological condition.
  • Vaccines: Biological preparations intended to stimulate protective immune responses against particular diseases.
  • Biosensors: Devices that use a biological element or biological recognition process to detect a specified substance or condition.
  • Protective research: Scientific work supporting personal protection, health monitoring and safer working conditions.
  • Environmental applications: Biological methods for studying or managing selected environmental problems.

These applications are important for civilians and can also contribute to medical preparedness for defence personnel. Their value depends on scientific validity, quality control, appropriate regulation and responsible use.

Indian defence life-sciences research

DRDO conducts research in life sciences as well as electronics and engineering. Its biomedical work includes areas related to human performance, protective technologies and medical support.

Examples of DRDO establishments include the Defence Institute of Physiology and Allied Sciences (DIPAS), which works on physiological and human-performance questions, and the Defence Research and Development Establishment (DRDE), associated with research relevant to biological and chemical defence and detection.

Defence life-sciences research should not be confused with the development of prohibited biological weapons. Protective and medical research serves different purposes and remains subject to applicable law and ethical requirements.

Biological risks and the dual-use problem

Scientific knowledge that can help diagnose or prevent disease may also raise security concerns if it is misused. This creates a dual-use research problem: the same general area of knowledge can support beneficial work while requiring safeguards against harmful applications.

Responsible governance includes suitable laboratory safety practices, research oversight, protection of sensitive information and lawful control of hazardous materials. The purpose is to enable beneficial science while reducing the risk of accidents or deliberate misuse.

Biological Weapons Convention

The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) is an international treaty prohibiting the development, production, acquisition, transfer, stockpiling and retention of biological and toxin weapons as defined by the Convention.

It was opened for signature on 10 April 1972 and entered into force on 26 March 1975.

The Convention does not prohibit legitimate peaceful biological research. It prohibits biological agents and toxins of types and in quantities that have no justification for prophylactic, protective or other peaceful purposes, along with the weapons-related activities covered by the treaty.

Prelims focus

  • Biotechnology has civilian, medical and defence-support applications.
  • Genetic engineering involves deliberate modification of genetic material.
  • Biosensors use biological recognition to detect specified substances or conditions.
  • DIPAS and DRDE are associated with DRDO life-sciences research.
  • The Biological Weapons Convention entered into force on 26 March 1975.
  • Trap: Peaceful biotechnology research is not automatically prohibited because biological knowledge can be misused.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, introduction and principles; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, medical applications and ethical issues; DRDO, Biomedical Engineering and Technologies, life-sciences research areas; United Nations Audiovisual Library of International Law, Biological Weapons Convention, Introduction and Treaty History. Official and institutional websites consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Defence Biotechnology, Medical Preparedness and Biological Security

body:
Why emerging technologies require governance

Technology governance refers to the rules, institutions and procedures used to guide the development and use of technology. In defence-related fields, governance must consider not only whether a technology works, but also whether it is reliable, lawful, safe and subject to appropriate human responsibility.

Artificial intelligence, autonomy, quantum systems, advanced sensing, biotechnology and strategic manufacturing create different risks. Consequently, a single technical rule cannot address every problem.

Reliability and accountability

A technology may function correctly during controlled tests but perform differently in unfamiliar environments. Reliable deployment therefore requires suitable testing, monitoring, maintenance and mechanisms for responding to failures.

Accountability means that people and institutions remain responsible for decisions and activities within their legal duties. Using software or automated equipment does not automatically remove human responsibility.

For example, a decision-support system may incorrectly identify an object in an image. The fact that the result came from AI does not establish that it was accurate or appropriate to act upon.

International humanitarian law

Where technologies are used in armed conflict, international humanitarian law (IHL) regulates the conduct of hostilities. Its rules apply to new means and methods of warfare as well as established ones.

Distinction

Parties to a conflict must distinguish between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Attacks must be directed only against lawful military objectives.

Proportionality

Even where a target is a lawful military objective, an attack is prohibited if the expected incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

Precautions

Parties must take feasible precautions in planning and conducting attacks to avoid, and in any event minimise, incidental civilian harm. The applicable requirements depend on the circumstances.

These principles matter when assessing autonomous weapon systems because software cannot be assumed to make every difficult legal and contextual judgment correctly. Existing IHL applies even when a system uses advanced automation or AI.

Human oversight is not merely the presence of a person near a machine. Effective oversight depends on whether responsible personnel can sufficiently understand, evaluate and control a system's use under the relevant conditions.

Other important governance questions

  • Privacy: Surveillance and data-processing systems may collect sensitive personal information. Lawful purpose, access controls and safeguards matter.
  • Cybersecurity: Software and connected equipment can be exposed to unauthorised access or manipulation.
  • Supply-chain security: Imported components and third-party software may create maintenance, reliability or security dependencies.
  • Research ethics: AI and biotechnology require attention to potential harm, misuse, bias and responsible oversight.
  • Export controls: Strategic technologies and dual-use items may be regulated because their transfer can affect national and international security.
  • Public accountability: Government procurement and public expenditure require appropriate oversight, even when some technical information must remain confidential.

Matching the technology to its principal concern

FieldPrincipal conceptImportant limitation or concern
Artificial intelligencePattern recognition and decision supportErrors, bias and accountability
Autonomous systemsActions within defined operating conditionsPredictability and human control
Quantum communicationQuantum-based communication security techniquesNot immunity from every cyberattack
Hypersonic technologyMotion at approximately Mach 5 or aboveTesting success differs from induction
Directed-energy technologyConcentrated electromagnetic energyOperating conditions, reliability and safety
BiotechnologyUse of organisms and biological componentsBiosafety, ethics and dual-use risks
Indigenous manufacturingDomestic production and supply capabilityForeign design or components may remain

Connecting Indian programmes with their functions

The following programmes represent different aspects of technological capability:

  • iDEX, launched in 2018: Defence and aerospace innovation involving startups and other innovators.
  • SRIJAN, launched in 2020: Identification of defence items for domestic development and import substitution.
  • DAP 2020: Capital acquisition with preference for indigenous procurement categories.
  • National Quantum Mission, approved in 2023: Research and technological development across quantum fields.
  • ADITI, launched in 2024: Support for critical and strategic defence technologies within the iDEX framework.
  • DPM 2025: Revenue procurement for equipment support, stores and services.
  • Positive Indigenisation Lists: Domestic sourcing of specified defence items according to notified timelines; the 6th DDP list was issued in August 2026.
  • SCOMET: Classification and export control of specified strategic and dual-use items.

These initiatives address different stages or needs. A research mission supports scientific development, a procurement procedure governs purchasing, an indigenisation list encourages domestic sourcing, and export controls regulate specified international transfers.

One-glance revision of the complete subject

The central relationship is that scientific research creates knowledge, industry develops production capability, testing establishes specified evidence of performance, procurement enables authorised acquisition, and governance regulates responsible use and transfer.

Dual-use technologies can contribute at several stages. AI can support analysis, quantum science can support communication and measurement, biotechnology can support health preparedness, and advanced materials and electronics can improve both civilian and defence equipment.

However, the terms developed, manufactured, tested, certified, contracted, exported and inducted identify different facts. They should not be treated as interchangeable descriptions of a project's progress.

Prelims focus

  • IHL requires distinction, proportionality and feasible precautions in the conduct of hostilities.
  • Existing IHL applies to autonomous weapon systems.
  • iDEX supports innovation; SRIJAN supports identification of items for indigenisation.
  • DAP addresses capital acquisition; DPM 2025 addresses revenue procurement.
  • SCOMET governs specified strategic and dual-use exports.
  • Trap: Research success, domestic manufacturing, certification, procurement and induction are different achievements.

[Sources: International Committee of the Red Cross, Frequently Asked Questions: Autonomous Weapon Systems, sections on international humanitarian law, distinction, proportionality and precautions, consulted 14 November 2026; DRDO, About DRDO, Mission; Press Information Bureau, Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020 announcement, 28 September 2020; Press Information Bureau, Defence Procurement Manual 2025 announcement, 23 October 2025; Department of Science and Technology, National Quantum Mission; Press Information Bureau, DDP 6th Positive Indigenisation List, 18 August 2026; Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Foreign Trade Policy 2023, Chapter 10, SCOMET. Official and institutional sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
